**2.3 Direct Threat.** A significant risk to the health or safety of others that cannot be eliminated by a modification of policies, practices, or procedures, or by the provision of auxiliary aids or services.

**2.4 Disability.** A physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a record of such an impairment, or being regarded as having such an impairment, as defined by the Americans with Disabilities Act Amendments Act of 2008.

**2.5 Reasonable Accommodation.** A modification or adjustment to a job, program, service, or environment that enables a qualified individual with a disability to have equal opportunity to participate. A reasonable accommodation is determined on a case-by-case basis and must not impose an undue hardship on the district.

**2.6 Service Animal.** A dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability.

**2.7 Undue Hardship.** An action requiring significant difficulty or expense when considered in light of factors including the nature and cost of the accommodation, the overall financial resources of the district, and the impact of the accommodation on district operations.

**SECTION 3: COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS**

The Accessibility Services Training Manual 2025-2026, effective date 2025-08-01, is the current district-wide accessibility policy. Record status: current.

**3.1 Legal Framework.** The district shall comply with all applicable federal and state laws, including but not limited to:

- Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, as amended
- Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
- The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA)
- State accessibility statutes and regulations

**3.2 Facility Accessibility.** All district facilities, including newly constructed, altered, or existing buildings, must comply with applicable accessibility standards. The district shall maintain an ongoing facility accessibility survey to identify and correct barriers. Priority shall be given to program access over architectural modifications where feasible.

**3.3 Digital Accessibility.** All district websites, web-based applications, electronic documents, and instructional materials must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA standards. The district shall conduct annual audits of digital content and shall remediate identified issues within a reasonable timeframe. New procurement of technology must include accessibility criteria in the evaluation process.

**3.4 Communication.** The district must provide effective communication to individuals with disabilities, including the provision of appropriate auxiliary aids and services where necessary. Requests for communication supports must be processed promptly and without discrimination.

**3.5 Program Access.** District programs and activities, when viewed in their entirety, must be readily accessible to and usable by individuals with disabilities. This requirement may be met through a variety of methods, including redesign of equipment, assignment of aides, home visits, or delivery of services at alternate accessible sites.

**3.6 Nondiscrimination.** No qualified individual with a disability shall, on the basis of disability, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any district program or activity. This prohibition extends to all employment practices, including recruitment, hiring, promotion, and termination.

**3.7 Complaint Procedures.** The district maintains grievance procedures for resolving complaints of discrimination based on disability. Complaints shall be investigated promptly and impartially. Retaliation against any individual who files a complaint or participates in an investigation is strictly prohibited.

**4. INCLUSION CLASSROOM OPERATIONS**

**4.1 Scope.** This section applies to all general education classrooms that include students with Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) or Section 504 Plans, hereinafter referred to as inclusion classrooms. The provisions of this section are intended to support the delivery of a free appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment.

**4.2 Maximum Class Size.** District Policy #504.2, maximum class size for inclusion classrooms 25 students, is stated in the policy document. Record status: current. No inclusion classroom shall exceed twenty-five (25) enrolled students at any point during the academic year, except as provided in Section 4.3 below. This limit applies to the total number of students on the official class roster, regardless of the number of students with disabilities assigned to that classroom.

**4.3 Exceptions and Override Procedures.** A school principal may request a temporary exception to the maximum class size when an enrollment surge occurs after the tenth instructional day of a semester. Requests must be submitted in writing to the Executive Director of Accessibility Services and must include:
- The specific classroom and current enrollment count;
- The projected duration of the exception, not to exceed fifteen (15) instructional days;
- A description of the additional supports that will be provided to maintain the quality of instruction;
- A plan for returning the classroom to compliance with Section 4.2.

**4.4 Composition and Staffing.** In determining the assignment of students to inclusion classrooms, the building principal, in consultation with the special education case manager, shall consider the overall composition of the class, including the range of instructional needs. Schools shall make every effort to distribute students with significant support needs equitably across sections of the same grade level or subject.

**4.5 Paraprofessional Support.** The assignment of paraprofessionals to inclusion classrooms shall be determined by the IEP team based on documented student needs. Paraprofessional assignments shall be reviewed at least once per grading period and adjusted as needed. Nothing in this section shall be construed to limit the district's obligation to provide a free appropriate public education as determined by each student's IEP.

---

**5. ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY**

**5.1 Definition.** Assistive technology (AT) includes any item, piece of equipment, or product system, whether acquired commercially, modified, or customized, that is used to increase, maintain, or improve functional capabilities of individuals with disabilities.

**5.2 Consideration Requirement.** Each IEP team shall consider whether a student requires assistive technology devices and services. This consideration shall be documented in the IEP. A separate assistive technology evaluation may be conducted when the IEP team determines that such an evaluation is necessary to make an informed decision.

**5.3 District Inventory.** The Accessibility Services Office shall maintain a centralized inventory of assistive technology devices owned by the district. The inventory shall record the device type, serial number, assigned location, and checkout status. Building-level AT contacts shall update the inventory at the end of each month and whenever a device is reassigned.

**6. TRAINING REQUIREMENTS**

**6.1 General Requirement.** All district employees who have direct contact with students shall complete accessibility awareness training annually. This includes teachers, paraprofessionals, administrators, clerical staff, custodial staff, and food service personnel. Training shall be completed no later than October 15 of each school year.

**6.2 New Employee Training.** New hires shall complete the accessibility awareness training module within thirty (30) calendar days of their start date. The building principal or department supervisor is responsible for ensuring that new employees are enrolled in the training within five (5) business days of hire.

**6.3 Specialized Training for IEP Team Members.** Staff who serve on IEP teams shall complete additional training on the IEP process, including the consideration of assistive technology and the documentation requirements described in Section 5.2. This training shall be completed every two (2) years and shall be offered at least twice each semester.

**6.4 Paraprofessional Training.** Paraprofessionals assigned to inclusion classrooms shall complete a minimum of twelve (12) hours of job‑specific training per school year. Topics shall include, but are not limited to, behavior intervention strategies, instructional support techniques, and the proper use of assistive technology devices assigned to the students they support. The building principal shall maintain documentation of completed training hours.

**6.5 Training Manual.** The Accessibility Services Office shall maintain a district‑wide training manual that contains the detailed content for all required training modules. The manual shall be reviewed and updated annually, and shall be made available to all staff through the district's learning management system. Building‑level administrators shall incorporate the manual's content into their local professional development calendars.

**6.6 Documentation.** All training completions shall be recorded in the district's professional development tracking system. Records shall include the employee name, position, date of completion, and the specific module completed. These records shall be retained for a minimum of five (5) years.

**8. GRIEVANCE PROCEDURES**

**8.1 General.** The district is committed to prompt and equitable resolution of complaints alleging discrimination on the basis of disability or alleging a failure to provide reasonable accommodations, auxiliary aids, or accessible facilities. This grievance procedure is intended to provide an internal mechanism for resolving such complaints without resorting to external proceedings.

**8.2 Who May File.** Any individual who believes they have been subjected to discrimination on the basis of disability, or who has been denied a reasonable accommodation, auxiliary aid, or access to a district program, service, or activity, may file a grievance. This includes students, parents, guardians, employees, and members of the public.

**8.3 Filing a Grievance.** A grievance shall be submitted in writing to the building principal or, if the grievance concerns a building‑level matter, to the district’s Accessibility Services Office. Grievances may be submitted using the district’s Accessibility Grievance Form, available at each school office and on the district website, or by letter or email. The grievance shall include:

- The name and contact information of the complainant;
- A description of the alleged discriminatory act or denial of accommodation, including the date and location of the incident;
- The specific accommodation or auxiliary aid requested, if applicable; and
- The remedy or resolution sought.

**8.4 Time Limits.** A grievance must be filed within thirty (30) calendar days of the alleged discriminatory act or denial of accommodation, or within thirty (30) calendar days of the date the complainant became aware of the act. The district may extend this time limit for good cause shown.

**8.5 Initial Review and Investigation.** Upon receipt of a grievance, the building principal or the Accessibility Services Office, as applicable, shall conduct an initial review. The complainant shall be notified in writing of the receipt of the grievance within five (5) school days. An investigation shall be completed within thirty (30) school days of receipt, unless the complexity of the matter requires additional time. If additional time is required, the complainant shall be notified in writing of the reason for the delay and the anticipated completion date.

**8.6 Resolution and Appeal.** The district shall issue a written decision to the complainant within ten (10) school days of the conclusion of the investigation. The decision shall include the findings of the investigation and, if a violation is found, the corrective action to be taken. The complainant may appeal the decision to the Superintendent or designee within fifteen (15) school days of the date of the decision. The appeal shall be reviewed and a written decision issued within twenty (20) school days of receipt.

**8.7 Confidentiality.** To the extent permitted by law, the district shall keep the identity of the complainant and the details of the grievance confidential. Information shall be shared only with those district employees who have a legitimate need to know in order to investigate and resolve the grievance.

**8.8 Retaliation Prohibited.** The district prohibits retaliation against any individual who files a grievance, participates in an investigation, or opposes a discriminatory practice. Any employee found to have engaged in retaliation shall be subject to disciplinary action, up to and including termination.

**8.9 Relationship to Other Procedures.** This grievance procedure is in addition to, and does not replace, other complaint procedures available under applicable law, including procedures under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. The district will inform complainants of the availability of other relevant procedures and of the right to file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, or other appropriate agency.

**3.2 Intake Meeting**

Within 10 school days of receiving a referral, the BAC shall convene an intake meeting with the parent. The purpose is to review the referral, explain the 504 process, and obtain written consent for evaluation. If the parent does not consent, the district may still proceed if it believes an evaluation is warranted, but only after providing the parent with prior written notice.

**3.3 Timeline**

The evaluation must be completed within 60 calendar days of receiving parental consent, unless the parent agrees in writing to an extension. Document any extension request in the student's file.

---

**Chapter 4: Evaluation and Data Collection**

The evaluation must be sufficient to determine whether the student has a disability and, if so, what accommodations are needed. There is no single required assessment instrument. The evaluation draws on information from multiple sources.

- Teacher observations and input
- Academic records and work samples
- Standardized test scores
- Medical or psychological reports (with parental consent)
- Attendance and behavioral records
- Input from the parent and, where appropriate, the student

**4.2 Evaluation Summary**

The BAC prepares a written Evaluation Summary (Form 504-E) that synthesizes the data. The summary must include:

- A statement of the data reviewed
- An analysis of whether a disability exists
- A description of the impact on major life activities
- A recommendation regarding eligibility

**4.3 Eligibility Determination**

The 504 team determines eligibility. This is not an individual decision. The team must include the BAC, at least one teacher familiar with the student, and a parent or guardian. The team reviews the Evaluation Summary and decides by consensus. If consensus is not reached, the BAC makes the final decision and documents the rationale.

---

**Chapter 5: Accommodation Plan Development**

If the student is found eligible, the team develops an Accommodation Plan. The plan is a written document that describes the specific accommodations, modifications, and services the student will receive.

**5.1 Meeting Requirements**

The plan is developed in a meeting with the same team members who determined eligibility. The meeting should be scheduled at a mutually agreeable time. Provide the parent at least seven days' notice, unless the parent agrees to a shorter timeline.

**5.2 Components of the Plan**

Each plan must include:

- Student name and date of birth
- Meeting date and attendees
- Statement of the disability and its impact
- List of accommodations, stated specifically
- Implementation responsibilities
- Review date (at least annually)
- Signatures of the parent, BAC, and a teacher

**5.3 Writing Accommodations**

Accommodations must be specific, measurable, and feasible. Avoid vague language such as "extended time as needed." Instead, write "extended time on tests, up to 50% additional time, in a separate setting." If an accommodation is not being implemented, the plan is not being followed. If an accommodation is not working, the plan should be revised, not abandoned.

**6.2 IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1**

The IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1, version number 3.1, is listed in the training manual. Record status: current. This template is used for students who receive special education services under an Individualized Education Program (IEP) and require accommodations that are not already embedded in the IEP goals and objectives. The IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1 is the current, authorized version for use during the 2025–2026 school year. Do not use the previous version (v3.0) or any earlier drafts. If you locate a file labeled "IEP Template v3.0" or "IEP Template v2.9," do not open it; contact the ASO and we will remove it from circulation.

The template is available on the ASO shared drive under the folder path: `S:\ASO\Templates\IEP\Accommodation_Plan_v3.1.docx`. A PDF version is also available for printing purposes, but all plans must be typed and submitted electronically unless a printing exception has been approved by the ASO.

**6.2.1 Template Fields**

The IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1 includes the following fields. Complete every field; an incomplete plan will be returned to the school for correction.

- Student legal name and date of birth
- Student ID number (as assigned by the district student information system)
- School name and school code
- Case manager name and contact information
- IEP meeting date (the date the plan was reviewed or developed)
- Plan effective date and review date
- Disability category (as listed in the IEP)
- Statement of the disability's impact on access to the general education curriculum
- List of accommodations, with each accommodation stated specifically
- Implementation responsibilities (who will provide each accommodation)
- Setting where each accommodation will be provided (e.g., general education classroom, resource room, separate setting)
- Frequency and duration of each accommodation (e.g., "for all unit tests," "daily during reading block")
- Signatures of the parent, the Building Accommodation Coordinator (BAC), and a teacher

**6.2.2 Writing Accommodations in the IEP Template**

The same principles from Section 5.3 apply to the IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1. Accommodations must be specific, measurable, and feasible. Avoid vague language such as "modified assignments as needed." Instead, write "assignments reduced to the essential learning objectives, with no more than 50% of the original problems, for the duration of the unit."

When documenting accommodations in the IEP template, follow these guidelines:

- Use action verbs and state the condition under which the accommodation is provided.
- Specify who is responsible for providing the accommodation.
- If an accommodation is provided in a separate setting, state the location and the staff member responsible for supervising the student.
- If an accommodation involves assistive technology, list the specific tool (e.g., "text-to-speech software, Read&Write for Google Chrome") and the training status of the student and staff.

**Example:**

> *Accommodation:* Extended time on tests, up to 50% additional time, in a separate setting.
> *Implementation:* The classroom teacher will provide the additional time. The BAC will arrange for a separate setting and a proctor. This accommodation applies to all unit tests and district benchmark assessments.

**6.2.3 Common Errors in Completing the IEP Template**

The following are the most common errors the ASO sees when reviewing submitted IEP Accommodation Plans. Review your plan against this list before submitting.

- **Error 1: Using the 504 template for an IEP student.** The 504 Accommodation Plan Template v4.2 is for students with a Section 504 plan, not an IEP. If the student has an IEP, use the IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1.
- **Error 2: Leaving the implementation responsibility blank.** Every accommodation must have a named person or role responsible for implementation.
- **Error 3: Writing "as needed" or "when appropriate."** These phrases are not specific enough. State the condition, frequency, and duration.
- **Error 4: Forgetting to date the plan.** The plan must include both an effective date and a review date.
- **Error 5: Using an outdated version of the template.** Only the IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1 is current for the 2025–2026 school year.
**7.3.2 Completing the Form**

The Assistive Technology Request Form must be completed by the student's case manager. The case manager is responsible for gathering the required information and obtaining signatures.

**Step-by-Step Instructions:**

1. **Download the form.** Go to the ASO intranet and select "Assistive Technology Request Form" under "Resources > Assistive Technology." Save the form to your computer.
2. **Complete Sections 1 and 2.** Enter the student's information and disability category. Use the student's legal name as it appears in the student information system.
3. **Complete Section 3.** Describe the AT device or service being requested. Be specific. For example, instead of "text-to-speech software," write "Kurzweil 3000, version 20, for reading and writing support." If the device is a trial device, note the trial start and end dates.
4. **Complete Section 4.** Summarize the team's discussion. Include any trials conducted, the length of the trials, and the results. If no trial was conducted, state why (e.g., "The student has used this device at home for two years and is proficient.").
5. **Submit the form.** Submit the completed form to the ASO AT Coordinator via email or interoffice mail. The form must be submitted **before** the applicable approval deadline (see Section 7.4).
6. **Await approval.** The ASO AT Coordinator will review the form and either approve or deny the request. The case manager will be notified of the decision via email.

> **Note:** Do not begin using an AT device or service with a student until the ASO AT Coordinator has approved the request. This includes trial devices. If a trial device is needed before approval, contact the ASO AT Coordinator to discuss an emergency trial request.

**7.4.1 Emergency Requests**

An emergency AT request may be submitted at any time. An emergency request is one where the lack of AT would cause immediate harm to the student or prevent the student from participating in a time-sensitive educational activity (e.g., a state assessment, a final exam).

To submit an emergency request:

1. Complete the Assistive Technology Request Form.
2. Write "EMERGENCY" in the subject line of the email or on the top of the form.
3. Submit the form to the ASO AT Coordinator.
4. Contact the ASO AT Coordinator by phone to alert them to the emergency request.

The ASO AT Coordinator will respond to emergency requests within one (1) business day.

**7.5 Review and Approval Process**

The ASO AT Coordinator reviews all AT requests. The review process includes the following steps:

1. **Completeness check.** The AT Coordinator verifies that all sections of the form are complete and that the required signatures are present.
2. **Eligibility check.** The AT Coordinator verifies that the student is eligible for services and that the requested device or service is consistent with the student's IEP or 504 plan.
3. **Technical review.** For software requests, the AT Coordinator checks that the software is compatible with district devices and that the district has the necessary licenses. For hardware requests, the AT Coordinator checks that the device is on the district's approved device list.
4. **Decision.** The AT Coordinator approves or denies the request. If the request is denied, the AT Coordinator will provide a written explanation and suggest alternative options.

This chapter outlines the step-by-step procedures for receiving, reviewing, and acting on requests for accessibility services. The intake process is the foundation of service delivery; accurate and timely documentation at this stage prevents delays in the implementation of accommodations and ensures compliance with federal and state regulations.

The procedures in this chapter apply to all campuses within the district. Any exceptions must be approved in writing by the Accessibility Services Office (ASO) Program Director. Questions about a specific student's situation should be directed to the ASO Intake Coordinator at the Central Office.

**9.2 The Intake Request**

**9.2.1 Who May Submit a Request**

A request for accessibility services may be initiated by any of the following:

- A parent or legal guardian
- A student (if 18 years of age or older, or an emancipated minor)
- A classroom teacher or campus administrator
- A school counselor or school psychologist
- An outside provider, with written parent consent

Requests must be submitted using the current **Student Accessibility Services Intake Form** (Form ASO-101, revised 06-2025). The form is available on the ASO website and from the front office at every campus. Staff should not accept requests made verbally or through informal notes; this ensures that all requests are documented consistently and that the required consent fields are complete.

**9.2.2 Required Components of a Complete Intake Packet**

A complete intake packet includes the following items. Use the checklist below to verify completeness before submitting the packet to the ASO.

| Item | Required? | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Form ASO-101, fully completed and signed | Yes | All fields must be completed. Incomplete forms will be returned to the campus. |
| Signed Release of Information (Form ASO-102) | Yes | Required for the ASO to contact outside providers. |
| Parent/guardian consent for evaluation (Form ASO-103) | Yes | This is separate from the Release of Information. |
| Vision and hearing screening results | Yes | Must be dated within the last 12 months. |
| Academic records, including report cards and any prior intervention data | Yes | At least two years of data, if available. |
| Documentation of any previous evaluations (e.g., psychological, medical) | If available | If not available, note this on the form. The ASO may proceed without it, but it may affect the timeline. |
| Teacher narrative describing observed needs | Recommended | Use the space provided on Form ASO-101, or attach a separate sheet. |

**Important:** Do not delay forwarding a packet to the ASO because a recommended item is missing. Forward the packet with the required items (marked "Yes" in the table above) and note the missing items in Section 6 of Form ASO-101. The ASO will determine whether the missing information is necessary before an evaluation can begin.

**9.3 Intake Processing Timeline**

The ASO follows the timeline below for all intake packets received after August 1, 2025. The timeline is measured in business days, which are Monday through Friday, excluding school holidays and scheduled breaks.

| Day | Action | Responsible Party |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Day 0 | Campus receives the completed intake packet and logs it into the Campus Intake Log (see Section 9.4). | Campus Accessibility Coordinator |
| Day 1 | Campus forwards the packet to the ASO Central Office via district courier or secure scan. | Campus Accessibility Coordinator |
| Day 3 | ASO logs the packet into the central tracking system and sends a written acknowledgment to the campus and to the parent/guardian. | ASO Intake Coordinator |
| Day 10 | ASO completes a preliminary review of the packet. If the packet is complete, the ASO assigns an evaluator and sends a Notice of Evaluation to the parent/guardian. If the packet is incomplete, the ASO sends a written request for missing information to the campus. | ASO Intake Coordinator |
| Day 15 | Campus responds to the request for missing information, if applicable. | Campus Accessibility Coordinator |
| Day 45 | Evaluation is completed and the evaluation report is drafted. | Assigned Evaluator |
| Day 60 | Eligibility determination is made, and the parent/guardian is notified in writing. | ASO Program Director |
**Chapter 10: Classroom Accommodations and Implementation Strategies**

Effective August 1, 2025

**10.1 Overview**

This chapter provides guidance on implementing the accommodations listed in a student’s
Section 504 Plan or Individualized Education Program (IEP). The procedures in this chapter
apply to all campuses in the district and to all instructional settings, including general
education classrooms, elective courses, physical education, field trips, and before- and
after-school programs sponsored by the campus.

The goal of accommodation implementation is to provide equal access to the curriculum and
to school activities so that a student with a disability can participate to the same extent
as a student without a disability. Accommodations are not modifications. An accommodation
changes *how* a student learns or demonstrates learning; a modification changes *what* a
student is expected to learn or demonstrate. If you are unsure whether an instructional
change is an accommodation or a modification, contact the Campus Accessibility Coordinator
(CAC) before making the change.

**10.2 Roles and Responsibilities**

| Role | Responsibility |
| :--- | :--- |
| Campus Accessibility Coordinator (CAC) | Serves as the primary point of contact for teachers and staff. Maintains the campus roster of students with accommodations. Provides training to staff. Monitors implementation. |
| Classroom Teacher | Implements accommodations in the classroom. Documents the use of accommodations. Communicates concerns to the CAC. |
| Special Education Teacher / Interventionist | Provides support for students with IEPs. Coordinates with classroom teachers on specially designed instruction. |
| Parent/Guardian | Receives notices of accommodation implementation. Participates in planning meetings. Reports concerns to the CAC. |
| Student | Participates in self-advocacy, as appropriate. Uses accommodations as needed. |

**10.3 The Accommodation Implementation Checklist**

Before the first day of school, the CAC will provide each classroom teacher with an
Accommodation Implementation Checklist (Form ASO-201) for each student on their roster.
The checklist is a summary of the accommodations in the student’s plan. It is not a
substitute for the plan itself. The teacher should review the full plan, which is available
in the student information system (SIS) under the “Accommodations” tab.

The teacher must complete the following steps by the end of the first week of school:

1.  Review the checklist and the full plan in the SIS.
2.  Sign the checklist to confirm receipt and understanding.
3.  Return the signed checklist to the CAC.
4.  If any accommodation appears unclear or impractical for the setting, note the concern
    in Section 4 of the checklist and schedule a time to speak with the CAC.

**10.4 Common Accommodation Categories**

The accommodations listed below are the most frequently used in the district. This list is
not exhaustive. An accommodation not listed here may still be appropriate for a student.
When in doubt, follow the student’s written plan.

**10.4.1 Presentation Accommodations**

These accommodations change how information is presented to the student.

| Accommodation | Example | Implementation Note |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Repeated directions | Teacher repeats the directions for an assignment or task. | Repeat the directions verbatim. Do not rephrase unless the student asks a question. |
| Larger print | Materials are printed in 18-point font or larger. | The CAC will provide digital copies of materials when available so the teacher can enlarge them. |
| Read-aloud | A teacher, aide, or text-to-speech tool reads text aloud to the student. | For assessments, follow the testing guidelines in Chapter 12. For classroom use, the student may use the tool independently. |
| Preferential seating | Student is seated near the teacher or the board. | Avoid seating the student near doors, windows, or other high-traffic areas unless the plan specifies this. |
| Visual supports | Use of graphic organizers, charts, or pictures. | The teacher or the student may create these. They do not need to be approved in advance. |
**Chapter 11: Documentation and Record Keeping**

Accurate and timely documentation is essential to the accessibility services program. Records
are used to plan services, communicate with families, monitor implementation, and demonstrate
compliance with federal and state requirements. This chapter describes the records that the
Accessibility Services Office (ASO) and Campus Accessibility Coordinators (CACs) create and
maintain, how long they must be kept, and the rules for sharing and destroying them.

**11.1 Records Created by the Accessibility Services Office**

The ASO maintains the official record for each student who receives accessibility services.
This record is separate from the student’s general education file and is stored in the secure
section of the student information system (SIS) under the “Accessibility” tab. The record
includes:

- The current accessibility plan (the written plan described in Chapter 3).
- All prior versions of the plan, marked with their effective dates.
- The original request for services and any supporting documentation from the family or a
  treating provider.
- The eligibility determination and the meeting notes from the initial eligibility meeting.
- Annual review meeting notes and any amendment forms.
- Logs of communication with the family about the plan, including attempts to reach the
  family when a meeting or signature is required.
- Records of any complaint or dispute and the resolution.

The ASO is responsible for the completeness of these records. A CAC who becomes aware that a
document is missing from a student’s record must notify the ASO within two school days.

**11.2 Records Created by the Campus Accessibility Coordinator**

The CAC keeps a working file for each student on their campus. The working file may contain
drafts, notes from hallway conversations, and other informal materials that are not part of the
official record. The working file must be kept in a locked cabinet or in a password-protected
folder on the campus network. The CAC must transfer the following items from the working file
into the SIS within five school days of the event:

- Completed accommodation checklists (see Section 10.3).
- Signed acknowledgment forms from teachers.
- Meeting notes from any team meeting about the student.
- Any written request from a teacher to clarify an accommodation.

Informal notes that are not transferred to the SIS must be destroyed at the end of the school
year, unless the CAC believes they may be needed for a dispute. In that case, the CAC should
attach the notes to the dispute record in the SIS.

**11.3 Retention Schedule**

The district follows the state records retention schedule for special education and related
services records. The table below summarizes the retention periods that apply to the records in
this chapter. Retention periods are counted from the end of the school year in which the
student last received services, unless a different starting point is noted.

| Record Type | Retention Period | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Current accessibility plan | Until the plan is replaced | The replaced plan becomes a prior version. |
| Prior versions of plans | Three years after the student leaves the district | |
| Eligibility determination and meeting notes | Five years after the student leaves the district | |
| Accommodation checklists and teacher acknowledgments | Three years after the student leaves the district | |
| Communication logs with the family | Two years after the last entry | |
| Complaint and dispute records | Five years after the dispute is resolved | |
| Working files (informal notes) | End of the school year | See Section 11.2 for exceptions. |

The ASO reviews the retention schedule each June and destroys records that have reached the end
of their retention period. Destruction must follow the method described in Section 11.6.

**11.4 Access to Records**

Access to a student’s accessibility record is limited to staff who have a legitimate educational
interest in the student. This includes the student’s teachers, the CAC, the school principal,
and the ASO staff. It also includes district staff who are conducting an audit or an
investigation, and the district’s attorneys when the record is relevant to a legal matter.
**12. Complaint and Grievance Procedures**

This chapter explains how complaints and grievances about accessibility services are
received, documented, and resolved. It applies to complaints from students, parents or
guardians, and staff, as well as grievances filed under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation
Act of 1973 and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The procedures in this chapter
are the current version, effective August 1, 2025.

**12.1 What Is a Complaint vs. a Grievance?**

A **complaint** is an expression of concern about a service, an accommodation, or the
behavior of a staff member. A complaint does not need to be in writing to be received, but
it must be documented by the Campus Accessibility Coordinator (CAC) or the Accessibility
Services Office (ASO) before it can be acted on.

A **grievance** is a formal, written allegation that the district has failed to provide a
required accommodation, has discriminated against a student on the basis of disability, or
has retaliated against a person for requesting an accommodation. A grievance must name the
student, describe the alleged failure or discrimination, and state the requested remedy.

The district encourages resolution at the lowest level possible. Most concerns are
resolved informally at the campus level. A grievance is appropriate when the concern is
not resolved informally or when the concern involves an allegation of discrimination or
retaliation.

**12.2 Who May File**

The following persons may file a complaint or grievance:

- A student with a disability;
- A parent or guardian of a student with a disability;
- A teacher or other district employee, when the complaint concerns a student’s
  accessibility services;
- An adult student, acting on their own behalf.

A parent, guardian, or adult student may designate another person to act as a
representative. The designation must be in writing and must be kept in the student’s
accessibility record.

**12.3 How to File a Complaint**

A complaint may be delivered in person, by telephone, by email, or in writing to the CAC
or to the ASO. The CAC must record the following information on the Complaint Intake
Form (Form ASO-12A):

- Date and time of the complaint;
- Name of the person making the complaint and their relationship to the student;
- Name of the student (if different from the person making the complaint);
- A description of the concern;
- The name of any staff member involved;
- The requested outcome, if any.

The CAC must provide a copy of the completed Form ASO-12A to the person making the
complaint within two school days of receiving the complaint.

**Example:** A parent calls the CAC to say that her child’s math teacher has not been
providing the extended time listed in the child’s accessibility plan. The CAC completes
Form ASO-12A over the phone, reads the description back to the parent to confirm it is
accurate, and emails a copy to the parent the same day. The CAC then contacts the math
teacher and the department chair to investigate.

**12.4 Informal Resolution**

The CAC is responsible for attempting to resolve a complaint informally within ten school
days of receiving it. The informal resolution process includes the following steps:

1. Review the student’s current accessibility plan and any relevant records.
2. Meet separately with the person making the complaint and any staff member involved.
3. Identify the cause of the concern and what can be changed.
4. Agree on a resolution and put it in writing.

If a resolution is reached, the CAC must complete the Informal Resolution Record (Form
ASO-12B) and provide a copy to all parties. The CAC must also enter a summary of the
resolution into the student’s record in the Student Information System (SIS) under the
“Complaint” tab.

If no resolution is reached within ten school days, the CAC must inform the person making
the complaint of their right to file a formal grievance and provide them with a copy of
the Grievance Form (Form ASO-12C).

**12.5 Formal Grievance Procedure**

**2.3 Direct Threat.** A significant risk to the health or safety of others that cannot be eliminated by a modification of policies, practices, or procedures, or by the provision of auxiliary aids or services.

**2.4 Disability.** A physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, a record of such an impairment, or being regarded as having such an impairment, as defined by the Americans with Disabilities Act Amendments Act of 2008.

**2.5 Reasonable Accommodation.** A modification or adjustment to a job, program, service, or environment that enables a qualified individual with a disability to have equal opportunity to participate. A reasonable accommodation is determined on a case-by-case basis and must not impose an undue hardship on the district.

**2.6 Service Animal.** A dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of an individual with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual, or other mental disability.

**2.7 Undue Hardship.** An action requiring significant difficulty or expense when considered in light of factors including the nature and cost of the accommodation, the overall financial resources of the district, and the impact of the accommodation on district operations.

**2.8 Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG).** The international standards for digital accessibility, currently at WCAG 2.1 Level AA as adopted by the district.

---

**SECTION 3: COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS**

The Accessibility Services Training Manual 2025-2026, effective date 2025-08-01, is the current district-wide accessibility policy. Record status: current.

**3.1 Legal Framework.** The district shall comply with all applicable federal and state laws, including but not limited to:

- Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, as amended
- Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
- The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA)
- State accessibility statutes and regulations

**3.2 Facility Accessibility.** All district facilities, including newly constructed, altered, or existing buildings, must comply with applicable accessibility standards. The district shall maintain an ongoing facility accessibility survey to identify and correct barriers. Priority shall be given to program access over architectural modifications where feasible.

**3.3 Digital Accessibility.** All district websites, web-based applications, electronic documents, and instructional materials must meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA standards. The district shall conduct annual audits of digital content and shall remediate identified issues within a reasonable timeframe. New procurement of technology must include accessibility criteria in the evaluation process.

**3.4 Communication.** The district must provide effective communication to individuals with disabilities, including the provision of appropriate auxiliary aids and services where necessary. Requests for communication supports must be processed promptly and without discrimination.

**3.5 Program Access.** District programs and activities, when viewed in their entirety, must be readily accessible to and usable by individuals with disabilities. This requirement may be met through a variety of methods, including redesign of equipment, assignment of aides, home visits, or delivery of services at alternate accessible sites.

**3.6 Nondiscrimination.** No qualified individual with a disability shall, on the basis of disability, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any district program or activity. This prohibition extends to all employment practices, including recruitment, hiring, promotion, and termination.

**3.7 Complaint Procedures.** The district maintains grievance procedures for resolving complaints of discrimination based on disability. Complaints shall be investigated promptly and impartially. Retaliation against any individual who files a complaint or participates in an investigation is strictly prohibited.

**4. INCLUSION CLASSROOM OPERATIONS**

**4.1 Scope.** This section applies to all general education classrooms that include students with Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) or Section 504 Plans, hereinafter referred to as inclusion classrooms. The provisions of this section are intended to support the delivery of a free appropriate public education in the least restrictive environment.

**4.2 Maximum Class Size.** District Policy #504.2, maximum class size for inclusion classrooms 25 students, is stated in the policy document. Record status: current. No inclusion classroom shall exceed twenty-five (25) enrolled students at any point during the academic year, except as provided in Section 4.3 below. This limit applies to the total number of students on the official class roster, regardless of the number of students with disabilities assigned to that classroom.

**4.3 Exceptions and Override Procedures.** A school principal may request a temporary exception to the maximum class size when an enrollment surge occurs after the tenth instructional day of a semester. Requests must be submitted in writing to the Executive Director of Accessibility Services and must include:
- The specific classroom and current enrollment count;
- The projected duration of the exception, not to exceed fifteen (15) instructional days;
- A description of the additional supports that will be provided to maintain the quality of instruction;
- A plan for returning the classroom to compliance with Section 4.2.

**4.4 Composition and Staffing.** In determining the assignment of students to inclusion classrooms, the building principal, in consultation with the special education case manager, shall consider the overall composition of the class, including the range of instructional needs. Schools shall make every effort to distribute students with significant support needs equitably across sections of the same grade level or subject.

**4.5 Paraprofessional Support.** The assignment of paraprofessionals to inclusion classrooms shall be determined by the IEP team based on documented student needs. Paraprofessional assignments shall be reviewed at least once per grading period and adjusted as needed. Nothing in this section shall be construed to limit the district's obligation to provide a free appropriate public education as determined by each student's IEP.

---

**5. ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY**

**5.1 Definition.** Assistive technology (AT) includes any item, piece of equipment, or product system, whether acquired commercially, modified, or customized, that is used to increase, maintain, or improve functional capabilities of individuals with disabilities.

**5.2 Consideration Requirement.** Each IEP team shall consider whether a student requires assistive technology devices and services. This consideration shall be documented in the IEP. A separate assistive technology evaluation may be conducted when the IEP team determines that such an evaluation is necessary to make an informed decision.

**5.3 District Inventory.** The Accessibility Services Office shall maintain a centralized inventory of assistive technology devices owned by the district. The inventory shall record the device type, serial number, assigned location, and checkout status. Building-level AT contacts shall update the inventory at the end of each month and whenever a device is reassigned.

**8. GRIEVANCE PROCEDURES**

**8.1 General.** The district is committed to prompt and equitable resolution of complaints alleging discrimination on the basis of disability or alleging a failure to provide reasonable accommodations, auxiliary aids, or accessible facilities. This grievance procedure is intended to provide an internal mechanism for resolving such complaints without resorting to external proceedings.

**8.2 Who May File.** Any individual who believes they have been subjected to discrimination on the basis of disability, or who has been denied a reasonable accommodation, auxiliary aid, or access to a district program, service, or activity, may file a grievance. This includes students, parents, guardians, employees, and members of the public.

**8.3 Filing a Grievance.** A grievance shall be submitted in writing to the building principal or, if the grievance concerns a building‑level matter, to the district’s Accessibility Services Office. Grievances may be submitted using the district’s Accessibility Grievance Form, available at each school office and on the district website, or by letter or email. The grievance shall include:

- The name and contact information of the complainant;
- A description of the alleged discriminatory act or denial of accommodation, including the date and location of the incident;
- The specific accommodation or auxiliary aid requested, if applicable; and
- The remedy or resolution sought.

**8.4 Time Limits.** A grievance must be filed within thirty (30) calendar days of the alleged discriminatory act or denial of accommodation, or within thirty (30) calendar days of the date the complainant became aware of the act. The district may extend this time limit for good cause shown.

**8.5 Initial Review and Investigation.** Upon receipt of a grievance, the building principal or the Accessibility Services Office, as applicable, shall conduct an initial review. The complainant shall be notified in writing of the receipt of the grievance within five (5) school days. An investigation shall be completed within thirty (30) school days of receipt, unless the complexity of the matter requires additional time. If additional time is required, the complainant shall be notified in writing of the reason for the delay and the anticipated completion date.

**8.6 Resolution and Appeal.** The district shall issue a written decision to the complainant within ten (10) school days of the conclusion of the investigation. The decision shall include the findings of the investigation and, if a violation is found, the corrective action to be taken. The complainant may appeal the decision to the Superintendent or designee within fifteen (15) school days of the date of the decision. The appeal shall be reviewed and a written decision issued within twenty (20) school days of receipt.

**8.7 Confidentiality.** To the extent permitted by law, the district shall keep the identity of the complainant and the details of the grievance confidential. Information shall be shared only with those district employees who have a legitimate need to know in order to investigate and resolve the grievance.

**8.8 Retaliation Prohibited.** The district prohibits retaliation against any individual who files a grievance, participates in an investigation, or opposes a discriminatory practice. Any employee found to have engaged in retaliation shall be subject to disciplinary action, up to and including termination.

**8.9 Relationship to Other Procedures.** This grievance procedure is in addition to, and does not replace, other complaint procedures available under applicable law, including procedures under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. The district will inform complainants of the availability of other relevant procedures and of the right to file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights, or other appropriate agency.

**3.2 Intake Meeting**

Within 10 school days of receiving a referral, the BAC shall convene an intake meeting with the parent. The purpose is to review the referral, explain the 504 process, and obtain written consent for evaluation. If the parent does not consent, the district may still proceed if it believes an evaluation is warranted, but only after providing the parent with prior written notice.

**3.3 Timeline**

The evaluation must be completed within 60 calendar days of receiving parental consent, unless the parent agrees in writing to an extension. Document any extension request in the student's file.

---

**Chapter 4: Evaluation and Data Collection**

The evaluation must be sufficient to determine whether the student has a disability and, if so, what accommodations are needed. There is no single required assessment instrument. The evaluation draws on information from multiple sources.

- Teacher observations and input
- Academic records and work samples
- Standardized test scores
- Medical or psychological reports (with parental consent)
- Attendance and behavioral records
- Input from the parent and, where appropriate, the student

**4.2 Evaluation Summary**

The BAC prepares a written Evaluation Summary (Form 504-E) that synthesizes the data. The summary must include:

- A statement of the data reviewed
- An analysis of whether a disability exists
- A description of the impact on major life activities
- A recommendation regarding eligibility

**4.3 Eligibility Determination**

The 504 team determines eligibility. This is not an individual decision. The team must include the BAC, at least one teacher familiar with the student, and a parent or guardian. The team reviews the Evaluation Summary and decides by consensus. If consensus is not reached, the BAC makes the final decision and documents the rationale.

---

**Chapter 5: Accommodation Plan Development**

If the student is found eligible, the team develops an Accommodation Plan. The plan is a written document that describes the specific accommodations, modifications, and services the student will receive.

**5.1 Meeting Requirements**

The plan is developed in a meeting with the same team members who determined eligibility. The meeting should be scheduled at a mutually agreeable time. Provide the parent at least seven days' notice, unless the parent agrees to a shorter timeline.

**5.2 Components of the Plan**

Each plan must include:

- Student name and date of birth
- Meeting date and attendees
- Statement of the disability and its impact
- List of accommodations, stated specifically
- Implementation responsibilities
- Review date (at least annually)
- Signatures of the parent, BAC, and a teacher

**5.3 Writing Accommodations**

Accommodations must be specific, measurable, and feasible. Avoid vague language such as "extended time as needed." Instead, write "extended time on tests, up to 50% additional time, in a separate setting." If an accommodation is not being implemented, the plan is not being followed. If an accommodation is not working, the plan should be revised, not abandoned.

**Chapter 6: Accommodation Plan Templates and Documentation (continued)**

**6.2 IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1**

The IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1, version number 3.1, is listed in the training manual. Record status: current. This template is used for students who receive special education services under an Individualized Education Program (IEP) and require accommodations that are not already embedded in the IEP goals and objectives. The IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1 is the current, authorized version for use during the 2025–2026 school year. Do not use the previous version (v3.0) or any earlier drafts. If you locate a file labeled "IEP Template v3.0" or "IEP Template v2.9," do not open it; contact the ASO and we will remove it from circulation.

The template is available on the ASO shared drive under the folder path: `S:\ASO\Templates\IEP\Accommodation_Plan_v3.1.docx`. A PDF version is also available for printing purposes, but all plans must be typed and submitted electronically unless a printing exception has been approved by the ASO.

**6.2.1 Template Fields**

The IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1 includes the following fields. Complete every field; an incomplete plan will be returned to the school for correction.

- Student legal name and date of birth
- Student ID number (as assigned by the district student information system)
- School name and school code
- Case manager name and contact information
- IEP meeting date (the date the plan was reviewed or developed)
- Plan effective date and review date
- Disability category (as listed in the IEP)
- Statement of the disability's impact on access to the general education curriculum
- List of accommodations, with each accommodation stated specifically
- Implementation responsibilities (who will provide each accommodation)
- Setting where each accommodation will be provided (e.g., general education classroom, resource room, separate setting)
- Frequency and duration of each accommodation (e.g., "for all unit tests," "daily during reading block")
- Signatures of the parent, the Building Accommodation Coordinator (BAC), and a teacher

**6.2.2 Writing Accommodations in the IEP Template**

The same principles from Section 5.3 apply to the IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1. Accommodations must be specific, measurable, and feasible. Avoid vague language such as "modified assignments as needed." Instead, write "assignments reduced to the essential learning objectives, with no more than 50% of the original problems, for the duration of the unit."

When documenting accommodations in the IEP template, follow these guidelines:

- Use action verbs and state the condition under which the accommodation is provided.
- Specify who is responsible for providing the accommodation.
- If an accommodation is provided in a separate setting, state the location and the staff member responsible for supervising the student.
- If an accommodation involves assistive technology, list the specific tool (e.g., "text-to-speech software, Read&Write for Google Chrome") and the training status of the student and staff.

**Example:**

> *Accommodation:* Extended time on tests, up to 50% additional time, in a separate setting.
> *Implementation:* The classroom teacher will provide the additional time. The BAC will arrange for a separate setting and a proctor. This accommodation applies to all unit tests and district benchmark assessments.

**6.2.3 Common Errors in Completing the IEP Template**

The following are the most common errors the ASO sees when reviewing submitted IEP Accommodation Plans. Review your plan against this list before submitting.

- **Error 1: Using the 504 template for an IEP student.** The 504 Accommodation Plan Template v4.2 is for students with a Section 504 plan, not an IEP. If the student has an IEP, use the IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1.
- **Error 2: Leaving the implementation responsibility blank.** Every accommodation must have a named person or role responsible for implementation.
- **Error 3: Writing "as needed" or "when appropriate."** These phrases are not specific enough. State the condition, frequency, and duration.
- **Error 4: Forgetting to date the plan.** The plan must include both an effective date and a review date.
- **Error 5: Using an outdated version of the template.** Only the IEP Accommodation Plan Template v3.1 is current for the 2025–2026 school year.

**7.3.2 Completing the Form**

The Assistive Technology Request Form must be completed by the student's case manager. The case manager is responsible for gathering the required information and obtaining signatures.

**Step-by-Step Instructions:**

1. **Download the form.** Go to the ASO intranet and select "Assistive Technology Request Form" under "Resources > Assistive Technology." Save the form to your computer.
2. **Complete Sections 1 and 2.** Enter the student's information and disability category. Use the student's legal name as it appears in the student information system.
3. **Complete Section 3.** Describe the AT device or service being requested. Be specific. For example, instead of "text-to-speech software," write "Kurzweil 3000, version 20, for reading and writing support." If the device is a trial device, note the trial start and end dates.
4. **Complete Section 4.** Summarize the team's discussion. Include any trials conducted, the length of the trials, and the results. If no trial was conducted, state why (e.g., "The student has used this device at home for two years and is proficient.").
5. **Submit the form.** Submit the completed form to the ASO AT Coordinator via email or interoffice mail. The form must be submitted **before** the applicable approval deadline (see Section 7.4).
6. **Await approval.** The ASO AT Coordinator will review the form and either approve or deny the request. The case manager will be notified of the decision via email.

> **Note:** Do not begin using an AT device or service with a student until the ASO AT Coordinator has approved the request. This includes trial devices. If a trial device is needed before approval, contact the ASO AT Coordinator to discuss an emergency trial request.

**7.4 Approval Deadlines**

Approval deadlines are established for each semester to ensure that devices and services are in place before the start of instruction. The deadlines apply to all AT requests, including new requests, renewals, and requests for device changes.

| Semester | Approval Deadline |
| --- | --- |
| Fall 2025 | September 15, 2025 |
| Spring 2026 | January 15, 2026 |

The Assistive Technology Request Form, approval deadline for Fall 2025 2025-09-15, is noted in the training manual. Record status: current. This deadline is current for the 2025–2026 school year. Requests submitted after the deadline will be reviewed for the following semester, unless an emergency exception is granted by the ASO Director.

**7.4.1 Emergency Requests**

An emergency AT request may be submitted at any time. An emergency request is one where the lack of AT would cause immediate harm to the student or prevent the student from participating in a time-sensitive educational activity (e.g., a state assessment, a final exam).

To submit an emergency request:

1. Complete the Assistive Technology Request Form.
2. Write "EMERGENCY" in the subject line of the email or on the top of the form.
3. Submit the form to the ASO AT Coordinator.
4. Contact the ASO AT Coordinator by phone to alert them to the emergency request.

The ASO AT Coordinator will respond to emergency requests within one (1) business day.

**7.5 Review and Approval Process**

The ASO AT Coordinator reviews all AT requests. The review process includes the following steps:

1. **Completeness check.** The AT Coordinator verifies that all sections of the form are complete and that the required signatures are present.
2. **Eligibility check.** The AT Coordinator verifies that the student is eligible for services and that the requested device or service is consistent with the student's IEP or 504 plan.
3. **Technical review.** For software requests, the AT Coordinator checks that the software is compatible with district devices and that the district has the necessary licenses. For hardware requests, the AT Coordinator checks that the device is on the district's approved device list.
4. **Decision.** The AT Coordinator approves or denies the request. If the request is denied, the AT Coordinator will provide a written explanation and suggest alternative options.

**Chapter 8: Fall 2025 Accessibility Training Series**

**8.1 Overview**

The Fall 2025 Accessibility Training Series provides required professional development for all school accessibility coordinators, paraprofessionals, and instructional staff who support students with disabilities. The series is designed to build foundational knowledge of accessibility services, refresh skills on documentation and reporting, and introduce new procedures for the 2025–2026 school year.

All sessions are delivered in a hybrid format. Participants may attend in person at the District Professional Development Center (Room 204) or join via the district's virtual meeting platform. Each session is 90 minutes unless otherwise noted. Attendance is recorded through the ASO training portal. Participants must check in within the first ten minutes of a session to receive credit.

The Fall 2025 Accessibility Training Series, start date 2025-10-06, is scheduled in the training manual. Record status: current. This start date is current for the 2025–2026 school year. All subsequent session dates in this chapter are confirmed as of the manual's publication date of August 1, 2025.

**8.2 Required Sessions**

All school accessibility coordinators and paraprofessionals must complete the following core sessions. Instructional staff who are not designated as coordinators are required to complete Sessions 1, 3, and 5 only.

| Session | Title | Date | Format |
|---------|-------|------|--------|
| 1 | Accessibility Services Overview and Legal Updates | October 6, 2025 | In person |
| 2 | Assistive Technology: Device Lending and Troubleshooting | October 20, 2025 | Virtual |
| 3 | Documentation and IEP Alignment | November 3, 2025 | In person |
| 4 | Emergency Procedures and Evacuation Planning | November 17, 2025 | Virtual |
| 5 | Communication and Collaboration with Families | December 1, 2025 | In person |
| 6 | End-of-Semester Reporting and Data Entry | December 15, 2025 | Virtual |

Sessions are scheduled from 3:30 PM to 5:00 PM Central Time. This time slot was selected to accommodate both school-day schedules and after-school staffing. If your campus has a conflicting commitment on a session date, contact the ASO Training Coordinator at least five business days in advance to request an alternate offering.

**8.2.1 Session Descriptions**

**Session 1: Accessibility Services Overview and Legal Updates**

This session covers the legal framework for accessibility services, including the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Participants will review the 2025–2026 ASO procedural updates and the updated service request timelines. This session is mandatory for all staff who are new to accessibility roles.

**Session 2: Assistive Technology: Device Lending and Troubleshooting**

This session provides hands-on training on the district's assistive technology lending library. Participants will learn how to check device availability, complete the loan agreement form, and perform basic troubleshooting. The session will also cover the procedures for reporting damaged or malfunctioning devices. Please bring your district-issued laptop or tablet to this session.

**Session 3: Documentation and IEP Alignment**

This session focuses on the documentation requirements for accessibility services. Participants will review the revised service log template (Appendix C) and practice writing progress notes that align with IEP goals. The session includes a guided exercise on converting a sample IEP accommodation into a measurable service log entry.

**Session 4: Emergency Procedures and Evacuation Planning**

This session covers the role of accessibility staff during emergency situations. Topics include evacuation routes for students with mobility impairments, shelter-in-place procedures for students with sensory sensitivities, and communication protocols with first responders. Each campus will receive a copy of the updated Emergency Planning Checklist for Accessibility Services (Appendix D).

**Chapter 9: Student Intake and Evaluation Procedures**

**9.1 Overview**

This chapter outlines the step-by-step procedures for receiving, reviewing, and acting on requests for accessibility services. The intake process is the foundation of service delivery; accurate and timely documentation at this stage prevents delays in the implementation of accommodations and ensures compliance with federal and state regulations.

The procedures in this chapter apply to all campuses within the district. Any exceptions must be approved in writing by the Accessibility Services Office (ASO) Program Director. Questions about a specific student's situation should be directed to the ASO Intake Coordinator at the Central Office.

**9.2 The Intake Request**

**9.2.1 Who May Submit a Request**

A request for accessibility services may be initiated by any of the following:

- A parent or legal guardian
- A student (if 18 years of age or older, or an emancipated minor)
- A classroom teacher or campus administrator
- A school counselor or school psychologist
- An outside provider, with written parent consent

Requests must be submitted using the current **Student Accessibility Services Intake Form** (Form ASO-101, revised 06-2025). The form is available on the ASO website and from the front office at every campus. Staff should not accept requests made verbally or through informal notes; this ensures that all requests are documented consistently and that the required consent fields are complete.

**9.2.2 Required Components of a Complete Intake Packet**

A complete intake packet includes the following items. Use the checklist below to verify completeness before submitting the packet to the ASO.

| Item | Required? | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Form ASO-101, fully completed and signed | Yes | All fields must be completed. Incomplete forms will be returned to the campus. |
| Signed Release of Information (Form ASO-102) | Yes | Required for the ASO to contact outside providers. |
| Parent/guardian consent for evaluation (Form ASO-103) | Yes | This is separate from the Release of Information. |
| Vision and hearing screening results | Yes | Must be dated within the last 12 months. |
| Academic records, including report cards and any prior intervention data | Yes | At least two years of data, if available. |
| Documentation of any previous evaluations (e.g., psychological, medical) | If available | If not available, note this on the form. The ASO may proceed without it, but it may affect the timeline. |
| Teacher narrative describing observed needs | Recommended | Use the space provided on Form ASO-101, or attach a separate sheet. |

**Important:** Do not delay forwarding a packet to the ASO because a recommended item is missing. Forward the packet with the required items (marked "Yes" in the table above) and note the missing items in Section 6 of Form ASO-101. The ASO will determine whether the missing information is necessary before an evaluation can begin.

**9.3 Intake Processing Timeline**

The ASO follows the timeline below for all intake packets received after August 1, 2025. The timeline is measured in business days, which are Monday through Friday, excluding school holidays and scheduled breaks.

| Day | Action | Responsible Party |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Day 0 | Campus receives the completed intake packet and logs it into the Campus Intake Log (see Section 9.4). | Campus Accessibility Coordinator |
| Day 1 | Campus forwards the packet to the ASO Central Office via district courier or secure scan. | Campus Accessibility Coordinator |
| Day 3 | ASO logs the packet into the central tracking system and sends a written acknowledgment to the campus and to the parent/guardian. | ASO Intake Coordinator |
| Day 10 | ASO completes a preliminary review of the packet. If the packet is complete, the ASO assigns an evaluator and sends a Notice of Evaluation to the parent/guardian. If the packet is incomplete, the ASO sends a written request for missing information to the campus. | ASO Intake Coordinator |
| Day 15 | Campus responds to the request for missing information, if applicable. | Campus Accessibility Coordinator |
| Day 45 | Evaluation is completed and the evaluation report is drafted. | Assigned Evaluator |
| Day 60 | Eligibility determination is made, and the parent/guardian is notified in writing. | ASO Program Director |

**Chapter 10: Classroom Accommodations and Implementation Strategies**

Effective August 1, 2025

**10.1 Overview**

This chapter provides guidance on implementing the accommodations listed in a student’s
Section 504 Plan or Individualized Education Program (IEP). The procedures in this chapter
apply to all campuses in the district and to all instructional settings, including general
education classrooms, elective courses, physical education, field trips, and before- and
after-school programs sponsored by the campus.

The goal of accommodation implementation is to provide equal access to the curriculum and
to school activities so that a student with a disability can participate to the same extent
as a student without a disability. Accommodations are not modifications. An accommodation
changes *how* a student learns or demonstrates learning; a modification changes *what* a
student is expected to learn or demonstrate. If you are unsure whether an instructional
change is an accommodation or a modification, contact the Campus Accessibility Coordinator
(CAC) before making the change.

**10.2 Roles and Responsibilities**

| Role | Responsibility |
| :--- | :--- |
| Campus Accessibility Coordinator (CAC) | Serves as the primary point of contact for teachers and staff. Maintains the campus roster of students with accommodations. Provides training to staff. Monitors implementation. |
| Classroom Teacher | Implements accommodations in the classroom. Documents the use of accommodations. Communicates concerns to the CAC. |
| Special Education Teacher / Interventionist | Provides support for students with IEPs. Coordinates with classroom teachers on specially designed instruction. |
| Parent/Guardian | Receives notices of accommodation implementation. Participates in planning meetings. Reports concerns to the CAC. |
| Student | Participates in self-advocacy, as appropriate. Uses accommodations as needed. |

**10.3 The Accommodation Implementation Checklist**

Before the first day of school, the CAC will provide each classroom teacher with an
Accommodation Implementation Checklist (Form ASO-201) for each student on their roster.
The checklist is a summary of the accommodations in the student’s plan. It is not a
substitute for the plan itself. The teacher should review the full plan, which is available
in the student information system (SIS) under the “Accommodations” tab.

The teacher must complete the following steps by the end of the first week of school:

1.  Review the checklist and the full plan in the SIS.
2.  Sign the checklist to confirm receipt and understanding.
3.  Return the signed checklist to the CAC.
4.  If any accommodation appears unclear or impractical for the setting, note the concern
    in Section 4 of the checklist and schedule a time to speak with the CAC.

**10.4 Common Accommodation Categories**

The accommodations listed below are the most frequently used in the district. This list is
not exhaustive. An accommodation not listed here may still be appropriate for a student.
When in doubt, follow the student’s written plan.

**10.4.1 Presentation Accommodations**

These accommodations change how information is presented to the student.

| Accommodation | Example | Implementation Note |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Repeated directions | Teacher repeats the directions for an assignment or task. | Repeat the directions verbatim. Do not rephrase unless the student asks a question. |
| Larger print | Materials are printed in 18-point font or larger. | The CAC will provide digital copies of materials when available so the teacher can enlarge them. |
| Read-aloud | A teacher, aide, or text-to-speech tool reads text aloud to the student. | For assessments, follow the testing guidelines in Chapter 12. For classroom use, the student may use the tool independently. |
| Preferential seating | Student is seated near the teacher or the board. | Avoid seating the student near doors, windows, or other high-traffic areas unless the plan specifies this. |
| Visual supports | Use of graphic organizers, charts, or pictures. | The teacher or the student may create these. They do not need to be approved in advance. |
